📖 Worked example — patent, trademark, or trade secret?

WORKED EXAMPLE — protect each asset correctly
• A novel compression algorithm you want exclusive rights to → patent (novel, non-obvious, useful; ~20 years; requires PUBLIC disclosure).
• The product name and logo customers recognize → trademark (renewable indefinitely while used and defended).
• The recommendation engine’s tuning parameters you never publish → trade secret (protection lasts as long as secrecy + reasonable measures: NDAs, access controls — but reverse engineering is lawful).
• The source code’s text itself → copyright, automatically.
One product, four regimes — matching asset to regime is the exam exercise.
⚠️ PATENT = DISCLOSE; SECRET = CONCEAL
They’re opposites: a patent trades disclosure for a time-limited monopoly; a trade secret trades no protection-from-independent-discovery for potentially forever. Coca-Cola’s formula = the canonical trade-secret example.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Beyond copyright, three other major IP regimes govern technology: patents (inventions), trademarks (brand identifiers), and trade secrets (confidential business information). Each has different requirements, durations, and enforcement. Knowing which regime fits which asset shapes how organizations protect and use IP.

Core concepts

1. Patents — exclusive rights in inventions. Granted by governments for new, useful, non-obvious inventions. US patent term is 20 years from filing. Holder can exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the invention. Disclosed publicly in the patent itself — the bargain is exclusivity in exchange for disclosure.

2. Patent types. Utility patents (most common; functional inventions). Design patents (ornamental designs of useful objects). Plant patents (new plant varieties). In software: utility patents covering processes and methods. Software patents are controversial — eligibility under Alice has narrowed significantly.

3. Patent infringement and defenses. Direct infringement: making, using, selling the patented invention. Defenses: patent invalidity (prior art, obviousness), non-infringement (your product doesn't read on the claims), exhaustion, license. Patent litigation is expensive — million-dollar minimum, often more.

4. Trademarks — identifying source. Words, logos, sounds, even colors that identify the source of goods or services. Apple's logo, Google's name, the Tiffany blue. Distinctiveness is required; generic terms can't be trademarks. Registration enhances rights but unregistered (common law) marks have some protection from use.

5. Trademark infringement and dilution. Infringement: use likely to cause consumer confusion about source. Dilution: weakening a famous mark even without confusion (using 'Coca-Cola' for a tractor brand). Genericide: a trademark becoming generic for a category and losing protection (escalator, aspirin).

6. Trade secrets — competitive secrets. Information that derives commercial value from being secret and is subject to reasonable protective measures. Customer lists, formulas, manufacturing processes, source code in some cases. No registration; protection lasts as long as the secret is kept. Enforcement against misappropriation, primarily through state law and the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act.

7. Choosing among regimes. An invention: probably patent, with some considerations of trade secret. A name: trademark. A creative work: copyright. A business process kept secret: trade secret. Many products use combinations — software code (copyright) implementing a patented algorithm running on machines whose name is trademarked, with internal documentation as trade secret.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Patenting things that should be trade secrets — disclosure is permanent.
  • Naming products generically and losing trademark protection.
  • Failing reasonable protective measures, then trying to enforce trade secret claims.
  • Assuming a patent gives you the right to practice your invention — it gives you the right to exclude others, not the right to act if someone else has a blocking patent.

Quick recap

Patents protect inventions through public disclosure plus 20-year exclusivity. Trademarks protect source identifiers (words, logos, colors). Trade secrets protect confidential information indefinitely as long as secrecy is maintained. Each regime fits different assets; many products use them in combination. Each has specific requirements and enforcement paths.

Glossary

Patent
Exclusive right in an invention, granted in exchange for public disclosure.
Trademark
Word, logo, or design identifying the source of goods or services.
Trade secret
Confidential business information protected as long as secrecy is maintained.
Prior art
Earlier disclosures relevant to whether a patent claim is novel.
Genericide
Loss of trademark protection when a mark becomes generic for a category.

📖 Worked example — plagiarism vs infringement, and license picking

WORKED EXAMPLE — two students, two libraries
• A student submits a blog post’s text as their essay WITH the author’s permission → not infringement (permission), still plagiarism (claiming credit). The two wrongs are independent: plagiarism = credit; infringement = rights.
• A developer ships a product embedding a GPL library → the copyleft condition requires releasing THEIR source under GPL too; embedding an MIT/Apache (permissive) library requires only attribution. Choosing a license IS choosing obligations — check before you import.
Open source = source available under license; it is NOT public domain (which has no owner/conditions at all).
⚠️ GPL IS “SHARE-ALIKE”
The one-line exam version: permissive (MIT/BSD/Apache) = use freely with attribution; copyleft (GPL) = derivatives must stay open under the same license. “Open source = do anything” is the trap.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work as your own — distinct from copyright infringement. Open source is the structured legal answer to 'how can software be shared and built upon while preserving authorship.' Both topics matter constantly in IT careers, from coursework to professional code reuse.

Core concepts

1. Plagiarism vs copyright infringement. Plagiarism: claiming credit for work that isn't yours. Copyright infringement: using copyrighted work without permission. They overlap but aren't identical — citing a paragraph (no plagiarism) without permission can be infringement; copying a public-domain work without attribution (no infringement) can be plagiarism.

2. Plagiarism in academic and professional contexts. Academic: typically grounds for failing the assignment, course, or expulsion. Professional: termination, reputational damage. Software contexts: presenting reused or AI-generated code as original is increasingly an explicit policy issue. Disclosure norms vary; when uncertain, disclose.

3. Self-plagiarism. Reusing your own previous work without disclosure. Permissible in some contexts (industry reuse), problematic in others (dual-publication of papers, recycling assignments across courses). Norms come from the specific community.

4. Open source licenses — the broad shape. Software licenses granting reuse rights subject to conditions. Permissive (MIT, Apache, BSD): minimal conditions, often just attribution. Copyleft (GPL): derivative works must be licensed similarly. Strong copyleft (AGPL): extends to network use. Weak copyleft (LGPL): linking exception. Each license is a tradeoff between freedom and reciprocity.

5. MIT, Apache, BSD — permissive licenses. Use freely, including in proprietary products, with attribution and license text. MIT is shortest. Apache 2.0 adds explicit patent grant. BSD has variants (2-clause, 3-clause). The default for most modern open source; minimal compliance burden.

6. GPL and copyleft. Use freely, but derivative works must be licensed under GPL. Designed to keep the work free. Strong implications for commercial use — combining GPL code into a proprietary product subjects the whole to GPL. GPLv2 vs v3 differ on patent and DRM clauses. AGPL extends copyleft to network-served software.

7. License compliance in practice. Track every dependency. Generate SBOMs. Note license obligations. Comply with attribution. Avoid mixing incompatible licenses. Tools (Black Duck, FOSSA, Snyk) automate much of this. Most organizations have policies; legal review for non-routine cases. Compliance failures lead to lawsuits and reputational damage.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing plagiarism (credit) and infringement (permission) — different harms, different remedies.
  • Pulling GPL code into a closed-source product — license violation that can require open-sourcing the whole product.
  • Trusting that 'on GitHub' means 'free to use' — many GitHub repositories have no explicit license, in which case the default is no reuse.
  • Removing attribution from open-source code to look 'cleaner' — direct license violation.

Quick recap

Plagiarism (credit) and copyright infringement (permission) are related but distinct. Both apply in IT. Open source licenses formalize software sharing — permissive (MIT, Apache, BSD) versus copyleft (GPL) versus strong copyleft (AGPL). Tracking and complying with license obligations is now standard engineering practice supported by SBOMs and scanning tools.

Glossary

Plagiarism
Presenting someone else's work as one's own, regardless of copyright status.
Permissive license
Open source license with minimal restrictions (MIT, Apache, BSD).
Copyleft license
Open source license requiring derivative works to be similarly licensed (GPL family).
AGPL
Affero GPL; extends copyleft to networked software services.
SBOM
Software Bill of Materials; inventory of dependencies and their licenses.

📖 Worked example — an AI bias case, root to remedy

WORKED EXAMPLE — the loan model that redlines
A credit model trained on historical approvals denies applicants from certain ZIP codes at twice the rate. Trace it:
• Root: historical data encodes past discrimination; ZIP is a proxy for protected class → training-data bias, not “evil code.”
• Detection: audit outcomes by group (disparate impact analysis).
• Remedies: remove/neutralize proxy features, rebalance data, fairness constraints, human review of edge cases, ongoing monitoring.
• Accountability: the DEPLOYER owns the outcome — “the algorithm decided” is not a defense; transparency/explainability duties attach to consequential decisions (credit, hiring, parole).
⚠️ BIAS IN, BIAS OUT — AT SCALE
The exam framing: AI doesn’t create prejudice, it AMPLIFIES what’s in the data, faster and wider than humans could. Detection + human accountability are the constant correct answers.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

AI systems make or shape decisions about hiring, lending, healthcare, criminal justice, and content moderation at scales no human team could match. The same scale that creates value creates risk: bias amplified, errors multiplied, accountability diffused. AI ethics is the discipline of taking these stakes seriously rather than treating them as future problems.

Core concepts

1. Sources of bias in AI. Training data: reflects historical patterns, including discriminatory ones. Annotation: who labeled the data and what they treated as 'correct.' Model design: optimization targets that proxy for what you actually want but aren't equivalent. Deployment: who the system is used on, in what context, with what oversight. Bias enters at every stage.

2. Disparate impact and protected classes. Even systems with no intent to discriminate can produce outcomes that disadvantage protected groups (race, gender, age, disability, others depending on jurisdiction). Disparate impact is actionable in employment and credit even without intent. Auditing for disparate impact is the working test.

3. Fairness has multiple definitions. Statistical parity: equal positive rates across groups. Equal opportunity: equal true-positive rates. Calibration: predictions equally accurate across groups. Predictive parity: equal positive predictive values. These are mathematically incompatible in general — you can satisfy one or two, not all. Choosing among them is itself a values decision.

4. Explainability and interpretability. Can you explain why the model produced this output? Linear models: yes. Decision trees: mostly. Deep neural networks: hard. LLMs: very hard. Regulated domains (credit, healthcare) often require explanation. Approaches: feature importance, SHAP values, counterfactuals. Trade-off between accuracy and explainability is real but smaller than it used to be.

5. Accountability for AI decisions. When an AI system produces a harmful decision, who is responsible? Developer? Deployer? User? The vendor? The model provider? Accountability tends to diffuse, which is itself a problem. Frameworks like the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and emerging case law are working out the lines.

6. Human-in-the-loop design. For consequential decisions — medical, legal, financial, hiring — human review before action is the standard ethical baseline. The human must have actual authority, time, and information to override; rubber-stamping doesn't count. Design choices determine whether HITL is real or theatrical.

7. Ongoing monitoring. Deployed AI drifts. Population changes, behavior changes, model performance shifts. Bias metrics that were acceptable at launch become unacceptable months later. Continuous monitoring of fairness, accuracy, and edge cases is engineering practice — fairness audits aren't one-time events.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • 'The model decided' as a defense — humans designed, trained, deployed, and accepted the model.
  • Treating fairness as solvable by removing the protected attribute — proxies remain (zip code, name, language).
  • Using AI for high-stakes decisions without explainability requirements that match the stakes.
  • Auditing once at launch and never again — drift and changing populations make this insufficient.

Quick recap

AI bias enters at every stage from data to deployment. Fairness has multiple incompatible mathematical definitions; choosing is a values decision. Explainability matters more in regulated and consequential domains. Accountability tends to diffuse and must be designed against. Human-in-the-loop and ongoing monitoring are the working ethical baselines.

Glossary

Algorithmic bias
Systematic skew in AI outputs reflecting training data, design, or deployment.
Disparate impact
Outcomes that systematically disadvantage protected groups, regardless of intent.
Fairness metric
Mathematical definition of fair outcomes; multiple definitions exist and are not mutually compatible.
Explainability
Ability to articulate why an AI system produced a specific output.
Human-in-the-loop
Workflow ensuring qualified human review before consequential AI-driven action.

📘 Deep dive: the case studies the OA cites

COMPAS: a recidivism-prediction tool shown by ProPublica to produce higher false-positive rates for Black defendants — the canonical algorithmic-bias case. Facial recognition: the Gender Shades study found error rates dramatically higher for darker-skinned women than light-skinned men — accuracy disparities across demographics. Job displacement: automation tends to displace specific TASKS and transform roles rather than simply replace all jobs; policy answers include retraining. Know each case and the lesson it teaches: biased training data produces biased outcomes.

Deepfakes are AI-generated synthetic audio/video that convincingly imitate real people — the countermeasures are detection tools and provenance labeling. Regulation: the U.S. has moved mainly through executive orders and agency frameworks (e.g., NIST), while the EU’s AI Act sets risk-based rules — fragmented vs comprehensive approaches.

📖 Worked example — social-media ethics flashpoints

WORKED EXAMPLE — four scenarios, judged
• An engagement algorithm boosts outrage because it maximizes watch time → the ethical issue is amplification incentives (harm as a side effect of the metric), plus misinformation spread.
• Infinite scroll + variable rewards designed to maximize time-on-app → addictive design; particularly scrutinized for minors.
• An influencer promotes a product without disclosing payment → deceptive advertising; FTC requires disclosure (#ad).
• Cyberbullying reports ignored by a platform → moderation duty vs scale; policies + reporting + protection of vulnerable users are the expected mechanisms.
The recurring structure: the metric being optimized (engagement/revenue) diverges from user well-being — name that divergence and the “ethical issue” question answers itself.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Social media platforms shape information flow, attention, mental health, and political discourse for billions of people. The platforms are private but increasingly function as public infrastructure. The ethical questions they raise — moderation, recommendation, manipulation, child safety — are the most-discussed technology ethics issues of the era.

Core concepts

1. The attention economy. Most major platforms monetize via advertising, optimized for engagement. Engagement-optimized recommendation tends to surface emotionally activating content — outrage, fear, novelty, controversy. The optimization is rational at the platform level and corrosive at the social level. Documented in research and platform internal documents.

2. Recommendation and amplification. Recommendation systems decide what hundreds of millions of people see. Even neutral algorithms produce outsized effects given that scale. Boundary cases — health misinformation, extremism, content involving minors — are where platforms accept accountability; the broader question of what content should be amplified is largely undebated within companies.

3. Misinformation and disinformation. Misinformation: false information spread without intent to deceive. Disinformation: deliberate. Both spread fast on social media because emotionally charged content gets engagement. Platforms have inconsistent records of slowing it. Labeling, fact-checking, throttling, removal — each tool has costs and limits.

4. Mental health and youth. Substantial research links heavy social media use to anxiety, depression, body image issues, especially in adolescent girls. Platforms have known about internal research showing these effects. Designing for engagement vs designing for well-being is an ethical tension built into the business model.

5. Coordinated inauthentic behavior. State-sponsored or politically motivated networks that use fake accounts, AI-generated personas, and coordinated tactics to manipulate discourse. Detection and removal is an ongoing arms race. The challenge: distinguishing coordinated inauthenticity from organic political organizing requires care to avoid suppressing legitimate speech.

6. The role of moderation. Every major platform moderates more than people realize — TOS violations, spam, child safety, illegal content. The question 'should platforms moderate?' is settled (yes, by economic and legal necessity). The question 'how should they moderate, by what rules, with what transparency and appeal?' is unresolved.

7. Engineer responsibility. Designers of recommendation systems, ad targeting, growth mechanics, and moderation pipelines make ethical choices that scale. 'Just optimizing the metric' doesn't absolve the choice of metric. Push for measuring downstream effects, raising concerns internally, and refusing the most harmful work — all part of professional ethics in this domain.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating algorithmic recommendation as 'showing what users want' — what they want is shaped by what's shown.
  • Assuming labeling and fact-checking are sufficient — corrections rarely catch up with the spread.
  • Designing for engagement metrics without considering downstream well-being effects.
  • Treating moderation as a binary 'should we' question rather than a 'how, what rules, what appeals' question.

Quick recap

Social media platforms operate as engagement-optimized attention economies. Recommendation systems amplify content at scale; the choice of metric is itself a values choice. Misinformation, mental-health effects, and coordinated inauthenticity are documented harms with imperfect fixes. Engineer responsibility extends to surfacing concerns and pushing for impact-aware metrics, not just executing on growth.

Glossary

Attention economy
Business model monetizing user attention, typically through advertising.
Engagement optimization
Algorithmic optimization for time spent, clicks, and reactions; correlated with emotionally charged content.
Misinformation / disinformation
False content spread unintentionally / intentionally.
Coordinated inauthentic behavior
Organized fake-account networks attempting to manipulate platform discourse.
Algorithmic amplification
The role of recommendation systems in disproportionately spreading some content.

Echo chambers: environments where you only see agreeing views, so beliefs harden. Filter bubbles: algorithms narrowing your feed to what you already engage with — the automated cause of echo chambers. Cyberbullying/harassment: repeated targeted abuse, amplified by anonymity and reach. Astroturfing: manufactured fake “grassroots” support — bought accounts and bots posing as organic public opinion.

📖 Worked example — autonomous systems & the digital divide

WORKED EXAMPLE — two policy analyses
The self-driving crash: who’s accountable — owner, manufacturer, software vendor? The ethical framework: manufacturers owe rigorous validation and transparency about limits (Level 2 vs Level 4 autonomy); regulators owe standards; “the car decided” doesn’t dissolve human/corporate responsibility. Same structure for autonomous weapons (human-in-the-loop debates) and medical AI (physician oversight).

The digital divide: a school district goes online-only; students without broadband/devices fall behind — access maps onto income/geography, compounding inequality. Remedies: infrastructure investment, subsidized access, device programs, offline alternatives. Frame: technology BENEFITS distribute unevenly unless access is treated as an equity issue.
⚠️ AUTONOMY NEVER ERASES ACCOUNTABILITY
Across cars, weapons, and diagnosis: the graded answer keeps humans/organizations responsible for the systems they deploy, with oversight proportional to stakes.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Two issues at the leading edge of technology ethics. Autonomous systems — vehicles, drones, weapons, decision systems — make choices without human-in-the-loop oversight, raising new questions about accountability and design. The digital divide, meanwhile, is the older problem now magnified: who has access to technology, who is left behind, and what equity looks like in a digitized world.

Core concepts

1. The autonomy spectrum. Most 'autonomous' systems aren't fully autonomous. SAE Level 0 (no automation) through Level 5 (full autonomy). Level 2-3 systems (advanced driver assistance) are deployed widely; Level 4-5 are limited. The hardest ethics issues sit at Level 3-4 where humans must intervene but rarely do — and may not be ready when they must.

2. The trolley problem and its limits. Famous thought experiment: should an autonomous vehicle harm one person to save many? Useful for discussion, misleading for design. Real autonomous systems face thousands of small probabilistic decisions per second, not one-shot life-or-death choices. The ethics of those small decisions, aggregated, matters more than the dramatic edge case.

3. Accountability for autonomous decisions. When an autonomous system causes harm, who is responsible? Manufacturer (defective design)? Software vendor (defective code)? Owner (improper use)? Operator (failure to monitor)? Liability frameworks are evolving via case law and statute. Strict product liability often applies, but novel scenarios stretch existing rules.

4. Autonomous weapons. Lethal autonomous weapons systems — drones, sentry guns, future systems — that select and engage targets without human authorization. Subject of intense international debate. Some governments deploy; others propose treaty bans. The ethical concerns: removing humans from the kill decision, escalation risks, accountability for war crimes, proliferation.

5. The digital divide. Differential access to technology and the skills to use it. Within countries: rural vs urban, low-income vs high-income, older vs younger. Between countries: vast gaps in connectivity, devices, and digital literacy. The divide compounds — those without access fall behind in education, employment, civic participation.

6. Equity in design. Design choices include or exclude. Apps that require always-on data exclude users with metered or absent connectivity. Interfaces designed for one language or literacy level exclude others. Voice assistants trained on majority accents fail with others. Equitable design considers who is being designed for and who might be designed out.

7. Bridging gaps. Public infrastructure investment (broadband, digital ID, libraries with internet). Affordable devices and connectivity. Digital literacy education. Localization and accessibility. None alone is sufficient; sustained policy plus design choices matter together. Engineers building consumer products participate in this through who they design for.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Designing autonomous systems for the trolley problem and ignoring the thousand small decisions per second.
  • Diffusing accountability for autonomous failures across so many parties that no one is responsible.
  • Building products for 'the average user' that effectively exclude those without high bandwidth or recent devices.
  • Treating the digital divide as a developing-country issue while ignoring urban-rural and income gaps within wealthy nations.

Quick recap

Autonomous systems span a spectrum and most consequential ethics happens in the middle of the spectrum, not at full autonomy. Real-world ethical decisions are aggregated probabilistic ones, not trolley problems. Accountability frameworks are evolving. The digital divide compounds inequalities; bridging it requires both public infrastructure and design choices that don't quietly exclude. Equitable design is itself an ethical practice.

Glossary

Autonomy spectrum
SAE Levels 0-5 ranging from no automation to full autonomy.
Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS)
Weapons that select and engage targets without human authorization.
Digital divide
Differential access to technology, connectivity, and digital skills across demographic groups.
Equitable design
Design practice considering who is included and excluded by default choices.
Strict product liability
Legal framework holding manufacturers liable for defects regardless of intent or negligence.

📖 Worked example — a hard framework-application question

WORKED EXAMPLE — when frameworks DISAGREE
A hospital AI triages ER patients. Optimizing survival-per-resource (utilitarian) deprioritizes the frailest patients; treating equal need equally (justice/duty) sacrifices aggregate outcomes.
The hard-question skill: (1) name each framework’s verdict AND its reasoning; (2) identify the value conflict (aggregate welfare vs individual equal worth); (3) propose the defensible synthesis — e.g., justice-based floors (no one denied care) with utilitarian optimization above the floor, plus transparency and appeal.
Full-credit answers show the conflict explicitly — single-framework answers to a two-framework question are the designed trap.

From Frameworks to Decisions

Ethical reasoning becomes useful only when you can apply a framework to a messy, real situation. Each major framework asks a different question. Utilitarianism asks: which action produces the greatest net good (benefits minus harms) across everyone affected? It is consequentialist and can, in principle, justify sacrificing an individual for aggregate welfare. Deontology asks: what duty or rule applies, regardless of outcome? Honesty, promise-keeping, and respecting persons as ends are binding even when breaking them would produce better consequences. Virtue ethics asks: what would a person of good character do, and what habits does this choice cultivate? Rights-based reasoning protects entitlements (privacy, consent, property) that cannot be overridden by mere utility. Social contract grounds obligation in the rules rational agents would agree to for mutual benefit. Ethical egoism holds that acting in one's own long-term self-interest is the right standard.

Decision Models and Whistleblowing

A structured model typically runs: recognize the ethical issue, gather facts, identify stakeholders and their stakes, generate options, evaluate options against multiple frameworks, choose and act, then reflect. Skipping fact-gathering is the most common failure. Whistleblowing is ethically justified when the harm is serious and probable, the whistleblower has exhausted or reasonably bypassed internal channels, has documented evidence a reasonable person would accept, and going public has a real chance of preventing the harm. Absent these, disclosure may be premature or self-serving. Watch for framework signals in the wording of a scenario: appeals to net outcomes signal utilitarianism, appeals to a rule that binds regardless of result signal deontology, and appeals to character or what a good engineer does signal virtue ethics.

📖 Worked example — a hard multi-domain scenario

WORKED EXAMPLE — one incident, four bodies of law/ethics
An employee’s misconfigured cloud bucket leaks EU patient data; a journalist finds it; the company’s lawyer suggests quiet deletion.
• Privacy law: GDPR (EU subjects) + HIPAA (health data) → mandatory breach notification with deadlines — quiet deletion is illegal.
• Ethics codes: honesty, avoid harm → disclose and remediate.
• Security practice: incident response — contain (secure the bucket), assess scope, notify, review.
• Speech/press: the journalist’s reporting is protected; suppressing it isn’t an option.
Hard questions braid domains; the method is to answer EACH domain, then reconcile — the reconciled action (notify + remediate + cooperate) satisfies all four.

Applying Security, Privacy, and Professional Norms

The CIA triad classifies security goals: Confidentiality (only authorized parties can read data), Integrity (data is accurate and unaltered), and Availability (authorized users can access systems when needed). A leaked customer list violates confidentiality; a tampered bank balance violates integrity; a ransomware lockout or DDoS violates availability. Mason's PAPA model frames information-ethics issues as Privacy (what info about me can be collected), Accuracy (who is responsible for errors), Property (who owns information and channels), and Access (who may obtain information).

Codes, Law, and Bias

The ACM/IEEE Code of Ethics obligates professionals to prioritize public welfare, be honest about capabilities and limitations, avoid harm, respect privacy and confidentiality, and give credit. GDPR principles include lawfulness and consent, purpose limitation (data collected for one purpose cannot be silently reused for another), data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, and the rights to access and erasure. Intellectual property splits into copyright (original expression such as code and text), patent (novel inventions/processes), trademark (brand identifiers), and trade secret (confidential business information kept secret, like an algorithm or recipe). Algorithmic bias can enter from biased training data (historical patterns), sampling/representation bias (groups under-represented), label/measurement bias (proxy targets), or feature bias (proxies correlated with protected traits). Informed consent requires disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, and capacity; buried defaults or coerced agreement fail it.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
